items.title: OpenAI - Fireside Chat with Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
items.desc:
We recently had the chance to chat privately with Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok about the impact of AI on the future of labor. One theme stood out: economic growth matters. It drives opportunity, innovation, and human flourishing.

Here's the conversation.
items.why: Cowen and Tabarrok discuss AI’s economic implications, innovation incentives, and growth prospects.

items.title: A Price Is a Signal Wrapped Up in an Incentive
items.desc:
Join Professor Tabarrok in exploring the mystery and marvel of prices. We take a look at how oil prices signal the scarcity of oil and the value of its alternative uses. Following up on our previous video, “I, Rose,” we show how the price system allows for people with dispersed knowledge and information about rose production to coordinate global economic activity. This global production of roses reveals how the price system is emergent, and not the product of human design. 

Microeconomics Course: https://mru.io/7de

Next video: https://mru.io/y4n

Help us caption & translate this video! http:
items.why: Explains how prices convey information and shape behavior through incentives—core to market coordination.

items.title: The Political Economy of Palestine (with Hussein Aboubakr Mansour)
items.desc: Most discourses about Israel or Palestine are morality plays of good guys vs bad guys. Egyptian-born Hussein Aboubakr Mansour takes a different approach, seeing the conflict as a self-reproducing system of political and economic extraction where Arab regimes, opposition movements, rival states, Western academics, NGOs, and Gulf monarchies like Qatar all convert Palestinian victimhood into their own forms of power, money, and meaning. Listen as Mansour speaks with EconTalk's Russ Roberts about his childhood in an Egypt organized around the liberation of Palestine and explores why any exit from
items.why: Analyzes the Israel-Palestine conflict through incentives, extraction, and international actors rather than morality narratives.

items.title: First reactions | Michael Woodford, prize in economic sciences 2026 | Telephone interview
items.desc:
“They're probably hoping I'll cancel the exam.” – Michael Woodford was scheduled to be setting his economics students an exam on the morning of October 12th, when he was woken by a call from Stockholm at 4:30am. Just after listening to the announcement of the 2026 prize in economic sciences, Woodford spoke to the Nobel Prize's Adam Smith about his feelings for the prize. He praised his co-laureate Robert E. Hall and explained why he admires the Swedish economist Knut Wicksell.

© Nobel Prize Outreach.

First reactions terms of use: https://www.nobelprize.org/ceremonies/streams-terms-of-use
items.why: A quick Nobel callback with Michael Woodford on his initial reactions and context for the prize.

items.title: Squawk Pod: Jeff Bezos & Andrew Ross Sorkin at Blue Origin - 05/20/26 | Audio Only
items.desc:
Jeff Bezos sits down with Andrew Ross Sorkin for an extended interview at the Blue Origin Rocket Park in Florida. In a wide-ranging conversation, the world’s fourth-richest person discusses America’s wealthiest class, U.S. tax policy, philanthropy, working with President Trump, and our country’s future. Bezos predicts AI-prompted deflation and an AI-prompted job shortage, and he doubles down on the concept of data centers in space. Plus, as owner of The Washington Post, Bezos comments on that newsroom’s mass layoffs and the current state of journalism. 

In this episode:
Jeff Bezos, @JeffBezos
items.why: A Bezos-market-economy defense with tax and AI labor/price predictions in a wide-ranging interview.

items.title: Announcement of the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel
items.desc:
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026 to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”.

The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was announced at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden.

#NobelPrize 

Live stream terms of use: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/about/live-streams-terms-of-use/
items.why: Concise announcement highlighting Hall and Woodford’s influential work linking micro foundations to stabilization policy.

items.title: Roman Mars on Flags, Phones, and the Design of Everyday Life
items.desc: Roman Mars has built one of podcasting’s great empires out of noticing things everyone else walks past. His show, 99% Invisible, has racked up over 500 million downloads telling stories about the unnoticed design choices that quietly shape how cities and objects work, from speed bump psychology and flag design to the shape of a good street sign. His TED Talk on vexillology (the study of flags) is so influential that it has reportedly spurred 250 to 300 municipal flag redesigns across the country, including in Pocatello, Idaho, a city he once publicly called out for having the worst flag in Ame
items.why: A fascinating design lens on how small features shape behavior in everyday urban life.

items.title: “One of the biggest policy questions we have in macroeconomics.” | 2026 economic sciences interview
items.desc:
“This year’s prize is about rebuilding a framework that allows us to study business cycles and stabilisation policy.” Following the announcement, Timo Boppart, member of the committee for the prize in economic sciences was interviewed by Owen Gaffney.  

© Nobel Prize Outreach
items.why: Explains a key macro question on modeling business cycles and evaluating stabilization policy.

items.title: Liaquat Ahamed on Financial Crises, Gold, and the Lessons of 1873
items.desc: Liaquat Ahamed has spent years making central bankers into compelling characters. His 2009 book Lords of Finance won the Pulitzer Prize for its account of the bankers whose decisions helped cause the Great Depression; his new book, 1873: The Rothschilds, the First Great Depression, and the Making of the Modern World, tells a stranger story — a severe deflationary crisis that barely dented global growth but poisoned politics for a generation. Tyler pushes him hard on the central puzzle of those two books — why did one financial crisis derail the world, while another left growth almost untouched
items.why: Explains 1873’s crisis through gold and finance networks, drawing lessons for later depressions.

items.title: Gita Gopinath on Trade, Currencies, and Economic Transformation
items.desc: Gita Gopinath has spent the last several years inside the room where the world's monetary plumbing gets fixed — or doesn't. As first deputy managing director of the IMF and, before that, the Fund’s chief economist, she worked on sovereign debt restructuring, followed Argentina’s disinflation up close, and built her academic reputation on ideas like dollar dominance and the dominant currency paradigm. Now back at Harvard launching a new Global Economics Lab, her conversation with Tyler ranges from why exchange rates don't adjust the way models predict, to what stablecoins really cost, to whethe
items.why: A high-level discussion of how currencies, trade, and global institutions shape economic transformation.

items.title: Luis Garicano on Spain, Europe, and the Future of Work
items.desc:
Luis Garicano has one of the more unusual résumés in economics: trained at the University of Chicago Booth School under Gary Becker, Kevin Murphy, and Sherwin Rosen, he left academia for a stint as a member of the European Parliament before returning to research, now at the London School of Economics for a second time. His new book, Messy Jobs, co-authored with Jin Li and Yanhui Wu, argues that AI won't cause mass unemployment for a surprising reason: it will make jobs messier, not simpler, and messiness is precisely what AI struggles with.

Tyler and Luis start their conversation with Spain —
items.why: Garicano connects Spain and Europe’s institutions to how technology reshapes jobs and inequality.

items.title: Free To Choose 1980 - Vol. 04 From Cradle to Grave - Full Video
items.desc: The welfare state arises from the attempt to do good with other people’s money. Such attempts always fail because: Nobody spends somebody else’s money as carefully as his own. Welfare is supply driven. Those spending the money use force to collect it and to insure those receiving it use it for ''right'' purposes. Good intentions are corrupted by bad means. Friedman visits U.S. and Britain. Discussion Participants: Robert McKenzie, Moderator; Milton Friedman; James R. Dumpson, Chief Administrator, Human Resources Admin., NYC; Thomas Sowell, Professor of Economics, UCLA; Robert Lampman, Professo
items.why: A Friedman/Sowell documentary critiquing welfare-state incentives and real-world failures in health and assistance programs.

items.title: Annie Lowrey on the Time Tax, Fraud, and Rationing by Paperwork
items.desc:
Annie Lowrey's new book, The Time Tax, argues that the most regressive levy in American life is the hours each of us must spend on hold, in waiting rooms, and filling out forms a competent state would have pre-filled — roughly fifty a year on average, and far more if you're poor. Tyler spends much of this conversation pressing the opposite case, asking whether that bureaucracy is quietly serving a useful purpose by rationing knee surgeries that don't work, deterring fraud, or screening for immigrants with gumption.

So Tyler and Annie hash it out over an hour, covering why TANF and other welfa
items.why: Explores how paperwork and administrative friction function like a regressive tax on the poor.

items.title: Jared Diamond on Leaders, Luck, and Irreplaceability
items.desc:
Is leadership overrated? That’s one simple reading of what Jared Diamond argues in his new book. Asked by Tyler to name the least replaceable leader in human history, Jared declines to name one — not Christ, the Roman Empire having had prophets to spare — and observes that even Genghis Khan happened to be born at an auspicious moment for a conqueror of the steppes. Conditions ripen; somebody turns up. So which leaders do make a difference?  

Tyler and Jared debate that question, including conditions what a religious founder needs to succeed, whether destructive leaders matter more than constr
items.why: A compelling debate on whether leaders drive history or whether luck and constraints dominate outcomes.

items.title: Michael Moritz on Origin Stories, Exile, and Obsessive Curiosity
items.desc:
Michael Moritz has written books through every phase of his life: the first history of Apple and an account of Chrysler's near-death while he was a journalist at Time, a study of Alex Ferguson's Manchester United in the middle of his 38 years at Sequoia, and now Ausländer, a family memoir, after leaving the firm. Moritz calls himself a dilettante with too many interests, but listen to him on learning to paint in his 40s, or the questions he would ask a ten-year-old boy in a German village in 1890, and you may decide that unsatisfied curiosity is not a small thing to build a life on.

Tyler and
items.why: A business-and-innovation memoir conversation connecting personal exile with company-building stories.

items.title: Daron Acemoglu on Liberalism, Automation, and the Educated Elite
items.desc:
Daron Acemoglu returns for his second appearance with a new book, What Happened to Liberal Democracy?, which Tyler reads as an attempt to redefine and revitalize liberalism for our times. Where Daron’s first visit was about how states and societies contend for the narrow corridor in which liberty survives, this one asks what liberals themselves got wrong, and the answer implicates the educated elite—that is to say, you.

Tyler and Daron discuss what's wrong with social contract theories and Rousseau's general will, whether Acemoglu is more objectivist than Rorty, why he blames left liberalism'
items.why: Acemoglu connects automation and inequality to failures in liberal institutions and elite incentives.

items.title: Luke Burgis on Mimetic Desire, Catholicism, and the Age of Social Contagion
items.desc:
Luke Burgis left Wall Street after two years, founded a few successful companies in his twenties, then walked away to spend three years in a Roman seminary on the path to the priesthood. He now runs the Cluny Institute and teaches at Catholic University. His book Wanting made René Girard legible to a general audience; the new one, The One and the Ninety-Nine, takes mimetic theory into the dynamics of self and crowd in an age of social contagion.

He joined Tyler to discuss whether the age of pessimism is ending, why the Anglo world in particular seems so unhappy, whether Dostoevsky or Thomas M
items.why: An engaging interview using Girard’s ideas to interpret desire, belief, and societal spread.

items.title: Julia Ioffe on Russian Women, Missing Men, and the Roots of Autocracy
items.desc: Julia Ioffe left the USSR as a child and came back as an adult journalist to find that the confident, credentialed women she remembered from her Soviet childhood had largely been supplanted by those chasing marriage and domesticity instead. That disorienting reversal is the engine of her book Motherland, a National Book Award finalist that reconstructs modern Russian history almost entirely through its women. Her account, drawn from her own family's history as well as the archives, keeps returning to one plain observation: Soviet policy pushed women into the workforce, the medical schools, and
items.why: Connects Soviet policy, gendered incentives, and social change to explain modern Russian autocracy.

items.title: Andrew Graham-Dixon on Vermeer, a Forgotten Sect, and Underrated Artists
items.desc: Andrew Graham-Dixon’s new book, Vermeer: A Life Lost and Found, rests on the conviction that you cannot understand what's in a painting without knowing what its maker was thinking about. In Vermeer's case, that context includes a forgotten liberal sect — the Remonstrants and Collegiants, Christians without a church who believed peace would come through reading and toleration rather than a returning Messiah. Recover that world and a woman alone in a sunlit room is a radical image in a Europe where half of Germany had just died in war. If he's right, the label beside every Vermeer in every museu
items.why: Art-history discussion tying Vermeer’s imagery to sectarian religious ideas and historical context.

items.title: Joel Mokyr on Clans, Corporations, and a Culture of Growth
items.desc: Joel Mokyr co-won the 2025 economics Nobel for exploring the question that traces back to the beginning of economics: how did sustained economic growth suddenly become normal? For nearly all of human history, cleverness didn't compound. What changed, according to Mokyr, was twofold: first, you need to know why something works, so that one advance can seed the next; second, you need a culture willing to tolerate the disruption. His new book contrasts Europe with China, showing how Europeans learned to cooperate with people they weren't related to, in guilds, monasteries, cities, and universitie
items.why: Explains why sustained growth took off, emphasizing knowledge chains and institutions that tolerate disruption.

items.title: 'The technological drivers of progress' - A podcast with the 2025 economic sciences laureates
items.desc:
We are living during a period of economic growth, but that hasn't always been the case. Throughout history, even during eras of technological advancements – economic growth was not a given. 

The 2025 laureates in economic sciences – Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt – help us to understand how scientific innovations and creative destruction impact society. 

Join us for this timely conversation where we discuss technological changes and the potential threats they cause.

This podcast was a production of Nobel Prize Outreach and Filt, and created in cooperation with Fundación Ramón
items.why: Top economists explain how innovation drives growth and restructuring, including the risks it creates.

items.title: Chase Koch on Principles, Music, and Overcoming Entropy | Conversations with Tyler
items.desc: Chase Koch grew up receiving Sunday philosophy lessons from his father Charles and, by his own account, spent most of them half asleep while his sister supplied the answers. The principles didn’t land until he lived them: throwing tennis matches as a bored teenager, getting shipped off to shovel manure at a feed yard twelve hours later, then spending five years battling Brazilian bureaucracy to build a fertilizer terminal that should have taken one. Today he is Executive Vice President of Origination and Partnerships, leader and donor to Stand Together, plays lead guitar in a band named for th
items.why: A philosophy-meets-business conversation focused on practical principles, perseverance, and navigating bureaucracy.

Born in East Germany in 1985 and now based in Britain, she has written acclaimed histories of the German Empire, the GDR, and most recently the Weimar Republic.

Tyler and Katja discuss why communism made East Germans more loyal to the system while it bred dissidents in Poland and Hungary, how happy or unhappy life in the GDR actually was, Tyler's own bleak day-trip to East Berlin in 1984, the underrated literature of the GDR (Christa Wolf, Bri
items.why: A historian explains Weimar and the GDR through politics, everyday life, and comparative communist experiences.

items.title: Joanne Paul on Thomas More and the Tudor World
items.desc:
Joanne Paul is a historian at the University of Sussex, author, and a go-to Tudor expert on YouTube. She tells Tyler she's drawn to the 16th century because it sits between the medieval and the modern, and because its paths not taken are a way of asking whether our own world had to turn out this way. Her biography Thomas More: A Life takes its subject in that spirit, refusing to reduce More to either martyr or monster.

Tyler and Joanne discuss how More influenced Erasmus, what to make of Utopia, why fear drove More's persecution of heretics, how Holbein's portraits of More and Cromwell differ
items.why: A thoughtful Tudor-focused conversation on Thomas More, faith, influence, and how to interpret Utopia.

Because minimum-wage policies do not necessarily reach the families most in need, the Earned Income Tax Credit provides a more targeted way to support low-income working families without limiting employment opportunities.

items.desc:
On October 12, Hoover Institution Senior Fellow Robert E. Hall was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences alongside Michael Woodford for groundbreaking research that transformed economists’ understanding of how the total mass of individual household and business decisions shape the broader economy.

items.title: Diarmaid MacCulloch on Christianity, Sex, and Unsettling Settled Facts
items.desc:
Tyler considers Diarmaid MacCulloch one of those rare historians whose entire body of work rewards reading. This work includes his award-winning Cranmer biography, his sweeping histories of Christianity and the Reformation, and his latest on sex and the church, which demonstrates what MacCulloch calls the historian's true vocation: unsettling settled facts to keep humanity sane.

Tyler and Diarmaid explore whether monotheism correlates with monogamy, Christianity's early instinct towards egalitarianism, what the Eucharistic revolution reveals about the cathedral building boom, the role of Mary
items.why: A historian-policy-adjacent discussion linking religion, institutions, and social norms through major historical research.

items.title: The Great Fertility Collapse with Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
items.desc: For the first time in human history, we're not having enough children to keep the world's population from falling. And fertility is collapsing fastest not in rich nations but in places like Colombia, Thailand, and Guatemala, upending decades of economic wisdom. Economist Jesús Fernández-Villaverde tells Russ Roberts, EconTalk host and Hoover visiting fellow, that falling fertility has accelerated sharply over the past decade and defies easy explanation. Declining religiosity, smartphones and social media, soaring housing costs, and changing gender norms are popular, but unconfirmed, theories.
items.why: Explores why fertility is falling worldwide and what it means for labor markets and future growth.

items.title: Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World
items.desc:
As of 2026, humanity is likely below replacement fertility. As far as we can tell, this has never happened before in our history as a species, not during wars, not during pandemics. Population keeps growing for another 30 years or so through momentum, and then it falls: our
reading puts the peak at roughly 9 billion around 2056.
• The UN WPP 2024 “Medium Variant” says 10.29 billion in 2084. I will explain why I disagree.
• China already records 3.3 million more deaths than births a year.
• But the real surprise is where the fall is happening.

To read the paper, click here: https://www.sas.upe

“I had a whole list of people that I thought were going to win,” says Joel Mokyr, “And I wasn’t on it.” Waking early, he opened up his computer to find out who had been awarded the 2025 prize in economic sciences, and found emails saying ’Congratulations.’ Then, as Mokyr tells the Nobel Prize’s Adam Smith in this brief call, he saw missed calls from Sweden on his phone and, “The suspicion started to ripen!”

© Nobel Prize Outreach.

First reactions terms of use: https://www.nobelprize.org/ceremonies/streams-terms-of-use
items.why: Quick Nobel reaction from Joel Mokyr—useful entry point to the year’s economics laureate.

items.title: The 2025 economic sciences prize: Did you miss the announcement?

items.why: Pure announcement coverage with no economic substance described.

items.title: First reactions | Philippe Aghion, prize in economic sciences 2025 | Telephone interview
items.desc: “Peter, Peter, make yourself available, your phone, they’re trying to reach you!” Listen to Philippe Aghion telling Peter Howitt that the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has been attempting to call him, captured as part of this call made shortly after the public announcement of their joint 2025 economic sciences prize. In this conversation with the Nobel Prize’s Adam Smith he also reveals his joy and surprise at the news, discusses the implications of their ‘creative destruction’ model of sustained economic growth, and suggests paths to ensuring that the fruits of growth can be more widely s
items.why: Aghion and Howitt briefly connect prize news to creative-destruction growth and broader sharing of benefits.

items.title: First reactions | Peter Howitt, prize in economic sciences 2025 | Telephone interview
items.desc:
“I’m not one of these people who keeps the phone on, and the champagne in the fridge.” Peter Howitt certainly didn’t seem to be expecting the news of his 2025 prize in economic sciences. In this call recorded just after the announcement, he talks to the Nobel Prize’s Adam Smith about his longstanding friendship with fellow-laureate Philippe Aghion and how they started their collaboration in the conducive environment of MIT. “My future,” he concludes, “is going to involve more economics, and less golf, than I had anticipated!” 

© Nobel Prize Outreach.

First reactions terms of use: https://www
items.why: Quick interview on prize-winning work, innovation, and how MIT shaped major research collaboration.

items.title: Jonny Steinberg on South African Policing, the Mandelas' Marriage, and the Post-Apartheid Era
items.desc:
Tyler considers Winnie and Nelson: Portrait of a Marriage one of the best books of the last decade, and its author Jonny Steinberg one of the most underrated writers and thinkers—in North America, at least. Steinberg's particular genius lies in getting uncomfortably close to difficult truths through immersive research—spending 350 hours in police ride-alongs, years studying prison gangs and their century-old oral histories, following a Somali refugee's journey across East Africa—and then rendering what he finds with a novelist's emotional insight.

Tyler and Jonny discuss why South African pol
items.why: Immersive reporting on South African policing and power transitions through Mandela-era personal and institutional history.

items.why: Evaluates California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax and its likely effects on investment and inequality.

items.title: Steven Pinker on Coordination, Common Knowledge, and the Retreat of Liberal Enlightenment
items.desc: Steven Pinker returns to Conversations with Tyler with an argument that common knowledge—those infinite loops of "I know that you know that I know"—is the hidden infrastructure that enables human coordination, from accepting paper money to toppling dictators. But Tyler wonders: if most real-world coordination works fine without recursively looping (a glance at a traffic circle), if these models break down with the slightest change in assumptions, and if anonymous internet posters are making correct but uncomfortable truths common knowledge when society might function better with noble lies, is
items.why: Pinker and Cowen explore how shared information underpins coordination and institutions across society.

items.title: Can America Still Deliver The American Dream?
items.desc:
Washington Post columnist Megan McArdle moderated a dynamic conversation with Hoover senior fellows John Cochrane (a.k.a. the Grumpy Economist and GoodFellow), Valerie Ramey, and Ross Levine on a defining question of the American experiment: why has the United States been such an enduring outlier in prosperity and can it remain so? For more than a century, America has been the world’s most prosperous large nation, yet confidence in the American Dream is faltering.

Don’t miss the next in-person conversation. Subscribe for daily insights and upcoming event updates: https://www.hoover.org/public
items.why: A research-informed debate on US prosperity, institutions, and whether the American Dream can endure.

items.desc:

How should we think about these vulnerabilities and their implications for economic and national security? How can we identify, assess, and respond to these vulnerabilities? Steven Davis asks two noted trade policy experts, Chad Bown and Soumaya Keynes.

items.title: John Amaechi on Leadership, the NBA, and Being Gay in Professional Sports
items.desc:
John Amaechi is a former NBA forward/center who became a chartered scientist, professor of leadership at Exeter Business School, and New York Times bestselling author. His newest book, It's Not Magic: The Ordinary Skills of Exceptional Leaders, argues that leadership isn't bestowed or innate, it's earned through deliberate skill development.

items.title: The Enduring Failures of Rent Control
items.desc:
Rent control promises to reduce housing costs, but in practice it constrains supply, degrades housing quality, and discourages new construction. Even after those failures become clear, the policy remains difficult to repeal because it protects those already in the market while leaving prospective tenants to compete for a shrinking supply.

Learn more from David R. Henderson:

items.why: Explains how rent control reduces supply and harms quality, and why repeal is politically hard.

items.title: David Brooks on Audacity, AI, and the American Psyche (Live at @92ndStreetY)
items.desc:
David Brooks returns to the show with a stark diagnosis of American culture. Having evolved from a Democratic socialist to a neoconservative to what he now calls "the rightward edge of the leftward tendency," Brooks argues that America's core problems aren't economic but sociological—rooted in the destruction of our "secure base" of family, community, and moral order that once gave people existential security.

Tyler and David cover why young people are simultaneously the most rejected and most productive generation, smartphones and sex, the persuasiveness of AI vs novels, the loss of audacity
items.why: A sociological take on AI-era incentives, culture, and human motivation with an economics-adjacent lens.

items.title: Stanford Econ Professor Pete Klenow on Business Cycles, Growth, Misallocation, and AI
items.desc:
Pete Klenow has spent his career tackling some of economics’ biggest questions: Why do some countries grow rich while others remain poor? What drives long-run prosperity? And how can policy foster innovation and productivity? In this episode of Capitalism and Freedom in the 21st Century, Jon Hartley sits down with the Stanford economist to discuss Klenow’s influential research on sticky prices, development accounting, economic growth, and the allocation of resources across firms and industries. 

Join our newsletter for more conversations like this: https://www.hoover.org/podcast/capitalism-an
items.why: A research-driven discussion of growth and cycles, with insights relevant to AI-era productivity.

items.title: From Scam Centers to Supply Chains: How the US is Meeting the China Challenge
items.desc:

They explain how the Commission monitors emerging risks, from advanced technologies like AI and quantum computing to vulnerabilities in supply chains and tracking scam centers abroad, culminating in a yearly report to Congress - and more. 

Tune into the next episode of China Considered by joining our newsletter: https://www.hoover.org/publications/goodfellows?utm_source=youtube&utm_m
items.why: A policy-focused discussion linking US China strategy, technology risk, and supply-chain vulnerabilities.

items.title: Online Buddies for Jobseekers
items.desc:
When job loss leads to a long spell of unemployment, it causes a big blow to self-esteem, a lasting drop in living standards, and serious hardship for the job loser’s family. Is there a low-cost way to help job losers navigate the search process and find rewarding new work? Yes, say two economists at Cornell University, based on their insightful new study. Steve discusses the study and underlying thinking with the authors.

items.title: Declining Industry and Public Trust at the Local Level: Elizabeth Elder on America’s “Company Towns”
items.desc:
What happens when an industry-dominant “company town” loses its primary employer? In the case of those parts of America once reliant upon coal companies to provide work and literally run small mining towns, Hoover fellow Elizabeth Elder has found economic hardship and a disturbing loss of confidence in democracy and institutions.

It's all chronicled in her new book, "Company Towns: Industry Power and the Historical Foundations of Public Mistrust." Learn more: https://www.hoover.org/research/declining-industry-and-public-trust-local-level-elizabeth-elder-americas-company-towns?utm_source=youtu
items.why: Explores how job loss in company towns erodes trust in democracy and local institutions.

items.title: Seamus Murphy on Photographing Patterns Across Cultures
items.desc:
Seamus Murphy is an Irish photographer and filmmaker who has spent decades documenting life in some of the world's most challenging places—from Taliban-controlled Afghanistan to Nigeria's Boko Haram territories. Having left recession-era Ireland in the 1980s to teach himself photography in American darkrooms, Murphy has become that rare artist who moves seamlessly between conflict zones and recording studios, creating books of Afghan women's poetry while directing music videos that anticipated Brexit.

Tyler and Seamus discuss the optimistic case for Afghanistan, his biggest fear when visiting
items.why: A thoughtful photojournalist conversation about documenting patterns of life amid conflict.

items.title: Nate Silver on Life’s Mixed Strategies
items.desc:

Tyler and Nate dive into expected utility theory and random Nash equilibria in poker, whether Silver's tell-reading abilities transfer to real-world situations like NBA games, why academic writing has disappointed him, his move from atheism to agnosticism, the meta-rationality of risk-taking, electoral systems and their flaws, 2028 presidential candi
items.why: A sharp discussion on prediction, risk, and decision theory tested against real-world data.

items.desc: Sure, you can use willpower or grit to break bad habits and build new ones. But maybe the key to success is simpler: change your situation. items.desc:

items.desc:

items.desc:

items.title: The Opioid Epidemic and US Political Realignment | Economics, Applied | Hoover Institution
items.desc:
Steven Davis speaks with Carolina Arteaga and Victoria Barone about the US opioid epidemic; specifically Purdue Pharma’s marketing strategy, its influence on physicians, and policy factors as drivers of the epidemic. items.desc:

items.desc: What if humanity's capacity for cruelty was actually one of our greatest moral achievements? items.title: Supply Constraints Do Not Explain House Price and Quantity Growth Across US Cities
items.desc:
The standard view of housing markets holds that differences in the flexibility of local housing supply—shaped by factors like geography and regulation—explain differences in how house price and quantity growth respond to rising demand across U.S. cities. However, from 2000 to 2020, we find that higher income growth predicts the same growth in house prices, housing quantity, and population regardless of a city’s estimated housing supply elasticity.

“Supply Constraints Do Not Explain House Price and Quantity Growth Across U.S. Cities”

By Johannes Wieland, Senior Research Advisor at the Federal
items.why: Challenges supply-constraint assumptions using citywide evidence linking income growth to housing prices and quantities.

items.desc: Introverts are underrated. So says Susan Cain in her conversation with EconTalk's Russ Roberts about her book, Quiet. items.desc:

Canada has gone through a lot in the last 10 years, and one of the biggest problems is the price of housing. Canadian cities are in such a small area of the country's landmass and housing construction has not kept up with the population, so housing prices have skyrocketed. Canada now finds itself in a bit of a population trap, where they can't afford to keep bringing in more people and put even more strain on housing, but they also can't afford not to.

items.desc: Amity Shlaes sheds light on the life of Calvin Coolidge, the thirtieth president of the United States. The harsh conditions of Coolidge's childhood shaped his political ideas and led to his deep understanding of life and helping people succeed, especially in business. Believing in small government and low taxes, he thought government needed to get out of the way so individuals and businesses could prosper. His supply-side economics were a resounding success, with an unemployment rate of 5 percent or even 3 percent, as the economy grew and the government shrank.
items.why: A political-and-economic profile of Coolidge arguing low taxes and limited government can boost prosperity.

items.desc:

items.why: Explains how blocksize limits trade off throughput to protect decentralization and privacy.
